title: a scripture that is the guru
hook: a scripture that is the Guru; why it's carried, covered, put to bed

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer, ending in sarbat da bhala. Your line was for everyone, not just us. Who did you wish well? Day twenty.

Late evening at a gurdwara. The last hymn has been sung. Someone gently closes a very large book, wraps it in embroidered cloth, and lifts it onto their head. Others walk ahead, sometimes calling out, while someone waves a whisk of long white hair over it, the way attendants once did for a king. The book is carried in procession to its own room, laid on a bed, and covered for the night. At dawn it's carried back out, unwrapped and opened, and the day begins. If you've never seen this, it can look astonishing. Why would anyone put a book to bed? Because on this path, the book isn't just a book. Today: a scripture that is the Guru.
screen: `A LARGE BOOK, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `PUT TO BED FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means book. Sahib is a word of deep respect. And Guru, the teacher you met on day two. The Guru who is a book. Here's how that happened. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him and his own, and in 1604 installed the collection at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Then, three days ago, we met Guru Gobind Singh. Near the end of his life, in 1708, the tenth Guru declared that there would be no more human Gurus. From then on, Sikhs would find their Guru in the scripture. So when Sikhs bow before it, they're bowing to the Guru, present in the words. That's why it's treated the way you'd treat a revered teacher in the room. It sits higher than everyone, on a small platform under a canopy. It's covered with cloth. Someone attends it with a whisk. It's put to rest at night and brought out at dawn. And inside? About fourteen hundred pages, which Sikhs call angs, limbs, as if of a body. Hymns by six of the Gurus. And, remarkably, hymns by holy poets who weren't Sikhs at all: Kabir, a weaver; Ravidas, from a caste many looked down on; Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. Their words sit in the scripture beside the Gurus'. Almost all of it is poetry, arranged by musical mode, meant to be sung. Every morning, many gurdwaras open it at random and read the first hymn on the page. It's called the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs don't only read this book. They listen to it, as to someone speaking to them today.
screen: `GRANTH — BOOK. SAHIB — RESPECT.` · `1708: NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `TREATED LIKE A TEACHER IN THE ROOM.` · `GURUS AND SAINTS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `A LIVING BOOK.`

segments.voice: Think of words that have spoken to you, a line from a book, a letter, something someone once said that you've never forgotten. Bring it to mind as exactly as you can. Now imagine those words not as something printed, but as someone sitting beside you, saying them to you now, today. Let them speak. Just listen. The bell holds the time.
The Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru since 1708, holding the Gurus' hymns and the words of other saints. Twentieth word.
Your line: a living book. Today, read one line of anything you treasure slowly, as if it were speaking to you right now. Day twenty.

howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy on a raised platform, is attended with a chaur, opened at dawn and put to rest at night; a hymn read at random each morning is taken as the day's hukamnama.

fork.setup: you're the tenth Guru, near the end of your life. who comes after you?
options: your chosen successor, the eleventh Guru.
the scripture itself, as the Guru.
fork.reveal: Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the Guru. that's why Sikhs bow to it, and why it's put to rest at night.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: guru (teacher) + granth (book) + sahib (a word of deep respect).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikh holy book.
what it means: the Guru itself, present in the words: honored like a living teacher, carried, covered and put to rest.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604; the final form adds the hymns of the ninth Guru. it runs to 1,430 angs, arranged by raga.

sources.ref: Sikh history on the Adi Granth (1604) and Guru Gobind Singh's declaration (1708)
Sikh Rehat Maryada (care of the Guru Granth Sahib; the hukamnama)

notes: Ravidas described as 'from a caste many looked down on'; confirm wording is respectful.
The chaur is compared to the whisk once waved for a king; confirm.

Hukamnama described as reading the first hymn on the page opened at random (the practice is to read the hymn beginning at the top of the left-hand page, or continuing from before). Confirm the simplification.
Six Gurus' hymns (Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Tegh Bahadur); confirm.
